summary: Proposes guidelines for designing Autonomic Service Agents for autonomic networks. Together with the Autonomic Network Infrastructure, Autonomic Control Plane, and GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol, they are base elements of an autonomic networking system. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Advice for building little helper programs that let a network manage itself.

questions: what is an autonomic service agent
subtitle: Design guidelines for autonomous agents that manage networks themselves

tldr.problem: Autonomic networks must include software agents that perform management tasks a human operator cannot do manually, such as continuous optimization and automated fault repair. But designing robust agents that coordinate with each other is complex.
tldr.mechanism: The document proposes guidelines covering agent structure (threads and initialization), interaction with the autonomic infrastructure (the control plane and signaling protocol), handling failures, security, coordination between agents, and the agent lifecycle (installation, instantiation, operation, removal).
tldr.outcome: Informational: provides a framework for designers building autonomic service agents within the autonomic networking ecosystem. No normative requirements.

today: RFC 9222 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It provides the current consensus on ASA design guidelines for autonomic networks. The autonomic networking ecosystem is evolving, with ongoing work on autonomic functions, GRASP extensions, and policy mechanisms.

sections.title: Autonomic Service Agents in Self-Managing Networks
sections.content:
An Autonomic Service Agent (ASA) is a software component that runs on a network device and performs an autonomic function—a task that adapts itself to changing network conditions without human intervention. ASAs implement network or service management, not user-facing services. Examples include agents that optimize resource allocation, detect and repair faults, or configure neighboring routers.

ASAs work within the Autonomic Network Infrastructure (ANI), which includes a secure control plane (the Autonomic Control Plane, or ACP), a discovery and signaling protocol (GRASP), and basic security through a bootstrap process (BRSKI). ASAs use GRASP to find each other, synchronize configuration, and negotiate over shared resources.

This document is guidance on how to design complex ASAs. Simple ASAs might manage a single parameter straightforwardly; complex ones coordinate across a distributed network and handle overlapping asynchronous operations.
sections.eli5: An autonomic service agent is a little program that lives on a network device and makes decisions on its own. This document gives advice on building them so they work well, talk to each other, and handle mistakes.

sections.title: Structure of an Autonomic Service Agent
sections.content:
A typical ASA has a main thread that does startup work: obtaining credentials, registering itself with GRASP, reading policy parameters, and declaring what objectives it will manage. Then the main thread enters a loop where it monitors conditions, sleeps for appropriate intervals, and refreshes credentials as needed.

For asynchronous operations (tasks that can happen in parallel), the ASA launches additional threads. These might flood an objective throughout the network, listen for synchronization requests, negotiate resource allocation with peer ASAs, or manage subsidiary devices. Each thread should exit when done or wait for new work to avoid wasting resources.

A self-monitoring thread is important: if an ASA fails despite careful coding, this thread detects the failure, attempts to fix it, and in the worst case restarts the entire agent. The main loop should also watch for policy changes and occasionally refresh security credentials.

This document describes a multi-threading model for clarity, but event-loop models and other asynchronous approaches are also valid.
sections.eli5: An ASA is like a worker with a supervisor. The worker has a main job (monitoring the network) and calls helpers when it needs to do several things at once. The supervisor watches to make sure the worker hasn't frozen or crashed.

sections.title: Integration with the Autonomic Ecosystem
sections.content:
Before ASAs can run, nodes are bootstrapped into a secure key infrastructure using BRSKI, which sets up the ACP. All ASA communication then flows through this protected channel.

GRASP is the core protocol for ASA communication. It offers registration (an ASA announces itself and the objectives it manages), discovery (finding other ASAs that support a given objective), negotiation (two ASAs exchange values back and forth until they agree), synchronization (one ASA requests the current value of an objective from another), and flooding (broadcasting an objective throughout the network).

ASAs interact with non-autonomic components too—a NETCONF server managing a router, for example. When multiple configuration tools might conflict, ASAs must coordinate to avoid inconsistency. ASAs may also interact with traditional management systems (SNMP, NETCONF, RESTCONF, command-line interfaces) and must account for these overlaps in their design.

Policy mechanisms for autonomic networks are still evolving. Each ASA must include sensible default values for all policy parameters so it can operate even without explicit policies.
sections.eli5: ASAs talk through a secure channel provided by the control plane. They use a discovery and negotiation protocol called GRASP to find each other and agree on how to share resources. They also have to talk carefully with traditional network management tools so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Agent Lifecycle
sections.content:
Installation: Software is loaded onto a device (including libraries) but not yet activated. Integrity and authenticity must be verified. An optional placement function allows the operator to specify which devices should host which ASAs.

Instantiation: ASA software is activated into a running instance. The operator provides an "Instance Mandate" specifying which resources the ASA will manage and what parameters to use (for example, an optimization target). The ASA discovers what resources it should control (if in "decoupled" mode, where control is separated from the location of the resource) and produces an "Instance Manifest" describing its managed resources and actions.

Operation: The ASA runs its control loops. The operator can activate or deactivate it, modify its targets, or update its managed resources. ASAs interact with other ASAs to exchange knowledge and collaborate on objectives. During this phase, coordination schemes prevent different ASAs from conflicting.

Removal: The ASA is uninstalled. All data and security key material must be purged.

The document emphasizes that seamlessly replacing a running ASA with a new version is essential for network continuity.
sections.eli5: An ASA's life has four stages: first it is installed (software loaded), then activated (told what to do), then it runs (doing its job), and finally it is removed (cleaned up).

sections.title: Making Agents Reliable
sections.content:
ASAs must be designed to survive failures. Even with careful coding, failures happen; the design should gracefully recover. Key robustness principles include:

Auto-restart with backoff: If an ASA encounters a fatal error, it should automatically restart. To avoid a restart loop on persistent failure, insert a suitable pause (with randomization and exponential backoff considered).

Safe bounds checking: If a received or calculated parameter is out of bounds, leave it unchanged or restore a known-safe value.

Repeatable operations: If a GRASP session fails, retry after a pause. If repeated failures suggest a peer has crashed, flush GRASP's discovery cache and re-discover peers. Periodically re-discover anyway, depending on the use case.

Message validation: Check all GRASP messages and objectives. Ignore wrongly formatted ones. For received objectives, verify syntax and semantics even if GRASP itself caught basic CBOR errors.

Extensibility handling: Objectives are likely to be extended with new fields in the future. ASAs should handle unknown components gracefully (ignore them, log and ignore, or reject as an error), as specified in the objective definition.

No unhandled exceptions: All exceptions should be handled in an orderly way.

A higher-level principle: design ASAs so that any error can be recovered from by returning to a known-good state rather than descending to a worse state—the "make-before-break" principle.
sections.eli5: Make agents tough: let them restart themselves, check values are sensible, retry when networks hiccup, and never leave things worse than they were.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
ASAs run inside an ACP that is protected by initial bootstrap (BRSKI) and provides secure communication channels. The ACP documentation and GRASP documentation cover broad security considerations. But ASAs also bear responsibility:

Prevent loopholes: When an ASA configures or manages resources outside the ACP (in a different node or across domain boundaries), it becomes a potential security loophole. An attacker could use it to penetrate the ANI boundary. ASAs must validate all incoming information, avoid passing executable code, and avoid proxying unverified commands.

Minimize privilege: ASAs should operate without special privilege when possible. When they must interact with management components like NETCONF servers, they should use secure coding practices and authenticate carefully.

Gateway vigilance: An ASA that acts as a gateway between two separate autonomic networks (accessing two separate ACPs) must validate information coming from both sides.

Transactional integrity: GRASP does not provide transactional integrity. ASA designers must account for the possibility of partial failures in negotiation.

Privacy: ASAs should consider relevant privacy implications per RFC 6973.

Fine-grained authorization: The current model assumes all ASAs on a node that has joined the ACP can manipulate any GRASP objective. Future work might add role-based authorization per node and per objective, but for now, limiting unnecessary privilege is the best practice.
sections.eli5: Since ASAs touch network configuration, security is critical. They should not reveal secrets, should check that commands are really from who they say they're from, and should never make network worse if something goes wrong.
